h1: Telling citrus, pine and tropical hop aromas apart in IPA
title: Citrus, Pine and Tropical Hops in IPA | Craft Beer School
desc: How to tell citrus, pine and tropical hop aromas apart in IPA, which hops give each and a simple tasting with fruit from the market.
teaser: Every IPA claims to be juicy and dank. Here is how to work out which hop aromas are really in the glass.
standfirst: Citrus, pine and tropical fruit are the three big families of hop aroma in IPA. They often appear together, which is why they blur. With a little practice and some fruit from the market, you can learn to pick each one out.
sections: Hop aroma comes from hop oil, a mix of compounds held in tiny yellow glands inside the cone called lupulin. A hop typically contains only a few millilitres of oil per 100 grams, yet that small amount carries most of an IPA's aroma. Different varieties carry different blends of oil, which is why a Cascade IPA and a Galaxy IPA smell so different. Our guide to how hops change aroma covers how timing in the brewhouse shapes the result.

Citrus is the classic American hop aroma. It ranges from grapefruit pith to orange peel to lime zest. Compounds such as linalool and geraniol play a part, along with others from the wider oil.

Hops known for it include Cascade and Centennial, which lean grapefruit. Amarillo leans orange. Citrus aroma tends to feel bright and sharp, with a slight bitterness like peel.

Pine aroma is green, sticky and resinous. Think pine needles, rosemary or the smell of a fresh-cut Christmas tree. It often comes with a dank, herbal edge. This family dominates many classic West Coast IPAs. Hops known for it include Simcoe, Chinook and Columbus.

Pine aroma often goes with firm bitterness. In a dry, clear IPA it can feel almost savoury. Our guide to West Coast IPA explains the style built around it.

Tropical aroma covers mango, passion fruit, pineapple, papaya and guava. Some of the most intense tropical notes come from thiols, a group of sulphur-containing compounds present in very small amounts that can smell of passion fruit, grapefruit or blackcurrant. Hops known for tropical character include Citra, Mosaic, Galaxy and Nelson Sauvin, which adds a white wine and gooseberry note.

Hazy IPAs lean heavily on this family. Our guide to New England IPA covers why the style tastes so soft and fruity.

Most hops do not sit neatly in one family. Citra gives grapefruit and mango at once. Simcoe can show pine and passion fruit. Brewers also blend two or three varieties in one beer. So the aim is not to name a single hop. It is to say which family leads and which supports.

Freshness matters too. Hop aroma fades quickly, especially in warm storage. Tropical notes are often the first to go. A three-month-old IPA that sat warm in an Indian summer may smell mostly of caramel and cardboard. Check the packing date before you blame the brewer.
A tasting with fruit from the market

Buy a small set of references: an orange, a lime or a sweet lime, some pine or rosemary, a ripe mango and a passion fruit or pineapple. Cut them and keep each in its own covered cup.

  1. Pour 100 ml each of two or three IPAs, ideally one West Coast and one hazy, at 7 to 10 °C in tulip glasses.
  2. Smell the first beer with short sniffs and write down your first impression.
  3. Smell each reference cup, then the beer again. The reference that seems to match or amplify the beer's aroma is a good clue.
  4. Repeat for each beer. Rest your nose by smelling the back of your hand between beers.

Keep pours small and share them. The point is to train your nose, not to drink three IPAs.

Aroma and bitterness come from different parts of the hop and different steps in the brewhouse. Bitterness comes mainly from alpha acids that are changed by the boil. Aroma comes from oils that boil away easily, so brewers add aroma hops late, in the whirlpool or during fermentation as dry hops. That is why a hazy IPA can smell intensely of mango but taste only gently bitter, while a West Coast IPA can be sharply bitter with the same hops.

When you taste, score aroma families and bitterness separately. It stops a strong bitterness from convincing you the beer smells of pine when it is really the citrus that leads.

Saying a beer smells "hoppy" tells nobody anything. Saying it leads with grapefruit pith and pine with a mango note underneath tells a brewer exactly what is in the glass. That precision comes from repeated work with references and a shared vocabulary. Our guide to beer aroma vocabulary is a good place to start building yours.
faqs: Cascade and Centennial are known for grapefruit, Amarillo for orange. Citra also gives citrus alongside tropical fruit.
What makes an IPA smell of pine?
Hop varieties such as Simcoe, Chinook and Columbus carry resinous, piney oils. They are common in West Coast IPAs.
Why do hazy IPAs taste tropical?
They use hops rich in tropical aromas, such as Citra, Mosaic and Galaxy. They are often hopped heavily late in the process to keep that aroma.
Why does my IPA not smell of much?
Hop aroma fades quickly, especially in warm storage. Check the packing date and buy IPAs from shops that keep them cold.
